topics: 🍽️ Eating Near the Dead — another room, a friend's house, a partition, or a turned face; no meat, wine or zimmun; Shabbat reverses it all
📍 'Laid Out Before Him' — Rav Pappa versus Rav Ashi: literal, or as long as burial is incumbent (Genesis 23:3–4)
👁️ Watching the Dead — exempt even for a stranger's corpse; two watchers alternate; ben Azzai's boat and the fear of mice
🪦 Four Cubits — tefillin and a Torah scroll in a cemetery: 'He who mocks the poor blasphemes his Creator' (Proverbs 17:5)
🦴 Dignity of the Dead — no riding on bones (or a Torah scroll), escorting a funeral, and Rabbi Yonatan's dragging tzitzit
💀 Do the Dead Know? — Ecclesiastes 9:5, the righteous who are 'living' in death (Benayahu), and the wicked who are 'dead' in life
👻 Three Cemetery Stories — the pious man and the two spirits, Ze'iri's innkeeper, and Shmuel's father in the yeshiva on high

overview.title: 📖 Overview: What the Dead Know
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 18a–18b
overview.hebrewSource: כִּי הַחַיִּים יוֹדְעִים שֶׁיָּמוּתוּ — אֵלּוּ צַדִּיקִים שֶׁבְּמִיתָתָן נִקְרְאוּ חַיִּים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens mid-baraita: one whose dead lies before him eats without reclining, meat or wine, is exempt from all mitzvot — but on Shabbat is obligated in everything. Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi reconcile this with the mishna's 'laid out before him', and the Gemara extends the exemption to anyone watching over a corpse, while limiting the cemetery prohibition to four cubits. A cluster of laws on the dignity of the dead follows: carrying bones, escorting a funeral, and Rabbi Yonatan's tzitzit dragging over graves. That last scene sparks the daf's great question — do the dead know what happens in this world? Rabbi Ḥiyya reads 'the living know they will die' as the righteous, and three stories — a pious man overhearing spirits, Ze'iri's innkeeper, and Shmuel's father — are weighed as proof, until Rabbi Yonatan himself retracts.

slides.title: 🍽️ Where Does the Bereaved Eat, and Why Is He Exempt?
slides.subtitle: The baraita's chain of fallbacks, and two ways to square it with the mishna

nodes.content: 📜 Baraita: one whose dead lies before him eats in another room → if none, a friend's house → if none, behind a partition → if none, he turns his face and eats

🚫 He does not recline, eats no meat, drinks no wine, recites no blessing and no zimmun, and is exempt from Shema, prayer, tefillin and all mitzvot. On Shabbat he reclines, eats meat, drinks wine and is obligated in all
❓ But the mishna exempts only when the dead is 'laid out before him' — and the baraita exempts him even in another house!

columns.label: Rav Pappa
columns.content: Read the exemption narrowly: it applies only to the case where he turns his face and eats with the dead before him

columns.label: Rav Ashi
columns.content: 'Before him' is not literal: since he is obligated to bury him, it is as if the dead lies before him — 'Abraham rose from before his dead… that I may bury my dead from before me' (Genesis 23:3–4)

callout.label: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's clause:
callout.text: 'Since he is obligated in these on Shabbat, he is obligated in all.' Rabbi Yoḥanan: the practical difference from the first tanna is conjugal relations — the first tanna forbids them on Shabbat, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel obligates.

slides.title: 👁️ Who Else Is Exempt — and How Far Does It Reach?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests the mishna's inferences against baraitot
rows: Watching over a corpse that is not one's relative
Exempt from Shema, prayer, tefillin and all mitzvot
Baraita — the mishna's 'his dead' and the baraita's 'watching' are complementary, not contradictory
His relative, but he is not watching
Same resolution: 'his dead even if not watching; watching even if not his dead'
Walking in a cemetery with tefillin and a Torah scroll
Prohibited within four cubits of a grave; beyond four cubits, obligated
'He who mocks the poor blasphemes his Creator' (Proverbs 17:5); 'the dead occupies four cubits for Shema'
His dead or one he is watching
The exemption is about his duty, not proximity
This one watches while that one recites, then they switch
Ben Azzai: set the corpse in one corner, both pray in another
Ravina: they differ over whether one fears mice on a boat

slides.title: 🦴 Honoring the Dead: Bones, Funerals, and Fringes
slides.subtitle: Three rulings on treating the dead — and a Torah scroll — with dignity

boxes.title: Carrying bones
items: One may not put bones in a saddlebag on a donkey and ride on them — that is disgraceful
If he fears gentiles or bandits, it is permitted
'As with bones, so with a Torah scroll' — this must refer to the leniency, since a Torah scroll is surely no less than bones

boxes.title: Escorting the dead
items: Raḥava in the name of Rav Yehuda: one who sees the dead and does not escort him transgresses 'He who mocks the poor blasphemes his Creator'
Rav Asi on the reward: 'He who gives to the poor gives a loan to the Lord' (Proverbs 19:17) and 'he who is gracious to the poor honors Him' (Proverbs 14:31)

boxes.title: Rabbi Yonatan's tzitzit
items: Walking in a cemetery with Rabbi Ḥiyya, Rabbi Yonatan's sky-blue fringe dragged over the graves
Rabbi Ḥiyya: lift it, so the dead do not say 'tomorrow they join us, and today they insult us'
Rabbi Yonatan: do the dead know so much? 'The dead know nothing' (Ecclesiastes 9:5)!

callout.label: Rabbi Ḥiyya's retort:
callout.text: 'If you read it, you did not repeat it; if you repeated it, you did not read it a third time; if you did, they did not explain it to you.'

slides.title: 💀 'The Living Know They Will Die' — Who Are the Living?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥiyya's reading of Ecclesiastes 9:5, and the sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya on Job 14

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya
lines.text: 'The living know that they will die' — these are the righteous, who even in death are called living: 'Benayahu son of Yehoyada, son of a living man' (II Samuel 23:20).

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: 'Son of a living man' — are all others sons of the dead? Rather, one who is called living even in death. 'Mighty deeds from Kabze'el' — he gathered many workers for Torah. 'Smote the two Ariel of Moab' — he left no equal in the First or Second Temple. 'Slew the lion in the pit on a snowy day' — he broke ice to immerse, or learned the Sifra of the school of Rav on a winter day.

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya
lines.text: 'The dead know nothing' — these are the wicked, called dead in their lifetime: 'you slain, wicked prince of Israel' (Ezekiel 21:30); or 'the dead shall be put to death' (Deuteronomy 17:6) — he is alive, so he is called dead from the outset.

lines.speaker: Son 1
lines.text: Rabbi Ḥiyya's sons, having forgotten their learning in the villages: does our father know of our anguish? 'His sons are honored yet he shall not know it' (Job 14:21).

lines.speaker: Son 2
lines.text: Does he not know? 'Only in his flesh does he feel pain, in his soul does he mourn' (Job 14:22) — and Rabbi Yitzḥak said maggots are as painful to the dead as a needle to living flesh.

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: They know their own pain, but do not know the pain of others.

slides.title: 👻 Three Stories, Three Rejections, One Retraction
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests whether the dead know the affairs of the living

steps.content: 1️⃣ The pious man gave a dinar to a poor man on Rosh HaShana eve in a drought year; mocked by his wife, he slept in the cemetery and overheard two spirits. One was 'buried in a mat of reeds' and could not roam; the other reported from behind the heavenly curtain that first-season sowing would be struck by hail

2️⃣ He sowed in the second season and his crops alone survived; the next year, the reverse (blight). His wife learned the secret, quarreled with the buried girl's mother, and taunted her about the reed mat. The third year the spirit said: leave me — our words have been heard among the living. So the dead know? Rejection: perhaps someone else died and told them

3️⃣ Ze'iri's innkeeper died holding his money. At her grave she told him: under the door hinge — and tell my mother to send my comb and eyeshadow with the woman who arrives tomorrow. Rejection: perhaps the angel Duma announces who is coming

4️⃣ Shmuel's father died with orphans' money; Shmuel was called 'son of the one who consumes orphans' money'. In the cemetery he found Levi sitting outside the yeshiva on high, barred for the years he had upset Rabbi Afes. Shmuel's father came crying (Shmuel will soon arrive) and laughing (Shmuel is important); Shmuel had Levi admitted

5️⃣ The money: in the millhouse — top and bottom ours, middle the orphans', so thieves would steal ours and the earth would eat ours. Rejection: perhaps Shmuel is different, and they announce 'clear a place' for one so important

6️⃣ Yet Rabbi Yonatan himself retracted: 'the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, saying' (Deuteronomy 34:4) — go tell the Patriarchs that the oath has been fulfilled for their children. The dead converse

summary.principle: The obligation to bury overrides every other mitzva while the dead awaits burial, the dead must never be mocked or disgraced — and the righteous, even in death, are called living.

flowSteps.content: 🍽️ Onen eats elsewhere or turns his face; no reclining, meat, wine, blessing or zimmun; exempt from all mitzvot — but obligated on Shabbat
❓ 'Before him' — Rav Pappa: only when turning his face; Rav Ashi: as long as burial is incumbent (Genesis 23:3–4)
👁️ Watcher of any corpse exempt; in a cemetery, tefillin and Torah scroll forbidden within four cubits — 'he who mocks the poor'

columns.content: 🦴 No riding on bones or a Torah scroll (except in danger); escort the dead; lift your tzitzit among the graves
💀 'The living know they will die' = the righteous (Benayahu); 'the dead know nothing' = the wicked

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Rabbi Yonatan retracted — the dead converse, as God told Moses to tell the Patriarchs their oath was fulfilled (Deuteronomy 34:4)

quiz.q: How does Rav Ashi reconcile the mishna's 'his dead laid out before him' with the baraita exempting one who eats in another house?
o: The baraita is a minority opinion and is rejected
'Before him' is not literal — as long as it is incumbent on him to bury the dead, it is as if the dead lies before him
The exemption applies only when he turns his face and eats
The baraita refers to Shabbat
quiz.e: Rav Pappa limited the baraita to the case of turning one's face, but Rav Ashi read 'before him' from Abraham: 'Abraham rose from before his dead' and 'that I may bury my dead from before me' (Genesis 23:3–4) — whenever burial is incumbent on him, it is as if the dead lies before him.

quiz.q: Why may one not walk within four cubits of a grave wearing tefillin and reading from a Torah scroll?
o: Because the cemetery is ritually impure
Because it is considered mocking the dead, who cannot perform mitzvot — 'He who mocks the poor blasphemes his Creator'
Because one might drop the Torah scroll
Because prayer is forbidden in a cemetery entirely
quiz.e: The baraita applies Proverbs 17:5 — performing a mitzva in front of the dead mocks those who can no longer perform mitzvot. The Gemara limits this to within four cubits; beyond that one is obligated.

quiz.q: According to Ravina, what is the practical difference between the first tanna (two watchers alternate) and ben Azzai (on a boat both may pray in another corner)?
o: Whether a boat counts as a private domain
Whether one is concerned about mice on a boat
Whether prayer may be recited while seated
Whether a corpse may be moved on a boat
quiz.e: Ravina explains the dispute turns on mice: the first tanna fears mice everywhere, so the corpse must never be left unwatched; ben Azzai holds there is no concern for mice on a boat.

quiz.q: What conclusion did Rabbi Ḥiyya's sons reach about whether their deceased father knew of their anguish?
o: The dead know nothing at all (Job 14:21)
The dead know everything that happens to their children
The dead know their own pain but not the pain of others
Only righteous fathers know of their sons' troubles
quiz.e: One son cited 'His sons are honored yet he shall not know it' (Job 14:21); the other cited 'in his flesh does he feel pain' (Job 14:22) and Rabbi Yitzḥak's statement that maggots pain the dead like a needle. They reconciled: the dead know their own pain but not others'.

quiz.q: From which verse did Rabbi Yonatan, after retracting, derive that the dead converse with one another?
o: 'And the dead know nothing' (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
'This is the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, saying' (Deuteronomy 34:4)
'His sons are honored yet he shall not know it' (Job 14:21)
'Son of a living man' (II Samuel 23:20)
quiz.e: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani reported that Rabbi Yonatan asked what 'saying' adds in Deuteronomy 34:4 — God told Moses: go tell Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that the oath I swore to you I have fulfilled for your children. This shows the dead converse.
